Trend Model Constructors for mvgam

Source: R/trend_system.R
trend_constructors.Rd

Specify trend models for multivariate State-Space models in mvgam. These constructor functions create trend specifications for various temporal dynamics including random walks (RW), autoregressive models (AR, VAR, CAR), local linear trends (LLT) and piecewise trends (PW). A constructor records its arguments. The model evaluates them against the data.

Usage

RW(
  time = NA,
  series = NA,
  ma = FALSE,
  cor = NULL,
  gr = NA,
  subgr = NA,
  n_lv = NULL,
  trend_map = NULL,
  df = Inf
)

AR(
  time = NA,
  series = NA,
  p = 1,
  ma = FALSE,
  cor = NULL,
  gr = NA,
  subgr = NA,
  n_lv = NULL,
  trend_map = NULL,
  coef_sharing = c("none", "shared", "hierarchical"),
  df = Inf
)

CAR(
  time = NA,
  series = NA,
  cor = FALSE,
  n_lv = NULL,
  trend_map = NULL,
  df = Inf
)

VAR(
  time = NA,
  series = NA,
  p = 1,
  ma = FALSE,
  cor = TRUE,
  gr = NA,
  subgr = NA,
  n_lv = NULL,
  trend_map = NULL
)

Arguments

time

The unquoted name of the numeric or integer variable in data that holds each row's time. Defaults to time.

series

The unquoted name of the factor variable in data that names each row's series. Its levels fix the order of the series. A trend needs this column even for a single series. Defaults to series.

ma

Logical. Include moving average terms of order 1? Default is FALSE.

cor

Logical. Include correlated process errors as part of a multivariate normal process model? If TRUE and if n_series > 1 in the supplied data, a fully structured covariance matrix will be estimated for the process errors. AR() and RW() default to NULL, which resolves to FALSE for an ungrouped trend and to TRUE whenever gr names a grouping variable: a grouped trend estimates correlations among the subgr units within each level of gr, which is the model gr exists to specify. VAR() and ZMVN() always estimate correlations and refuse cor = FALSE, as do AR(gr = ...) and RW(gr = ...). CAR() defaults to FALSE.

gr

An optional grouping variable, which must be a factor in the supplied data, for setting up hierarchical residual correlation structures. If specified, this sets up a model where the residual correlations for a specific level of gr are modelled hierarchically:

\(\Omega_{group} = \alpha_{cor}\Omega_{global} + (1 - \alpha_{cor})\Omega_{group, local}\),

where \(\Omega_{global}\) is a global correlation matrix, \(\Omega_{group, local}\) is a local deviation correlation matrix and \(\alpha_{cor}\) is a weighting parameter controlling how strongly the local correlation matrix \(\Omega_{group}\) is shrunk towards the global correlation matrix \(\Omega_{global}\) (larger values of \(\alpha_{cor}\) indicate a greater degree of shrinkage, i.e. a greater degree of partial pooling).

A grouped trend estimates correlations among the subgr units within each level of gr. Without subgr, the series column names those units. cor defaults to TRUE for such a trend. An explicit cor = FALSE is refused.

Within a VAR() it sets up a hierarchical panel vector autoregression. Each group learns its autoregressive, moving-average and correlation matrices from shared hyperparameters. The groups do not interact.

Two constraints apply to hierarchical trend models:

  • gr must be constant within each series (each series belongs to a single group). Models with gr varying within a series are rejected at validation time.

  • Every group must hold the same number of series. The Stan program sizes each group's correlation block from one shared count. Validation refuses unbalanced groups before fitting.

subgr

A subgrouping factor variable naming the time series within each level of gr. Defaults to series. A model with hierarchical correlations builds its series from gr and subgr, and data then needs no series column.

For example, to model counts of several species (species in data) across three regions (region) with residuals correlated within regions, specify gr = region and subgr = species. mvgam() then builds the series as

series = interaction(gr, subgr, drop = TRUE, sep = "_", lex.order = TRUE)

A region r1 and a species sp1 give the series "r1_sp1". The levels sort lexically. summary(), plot() and forecast() all label that series "r1_sp1". A series column that disagrees with the derived series is replaced by it, with a warning.

n_lv

The number of latent factors to estimate for dynamic factor models. When n_lv is smaller than the number of series, the latent processes are modelled as n_lv factors with estimated loadings onto the series. Defaults to NULL, in which case one latent process is used per series.

trend_map

Optional specification of which latent process each series maps onto. It fixes the loadings of a dynamic factor model. See mvgam for the accepted formats. Defaults to NULL.

df

Degrees of freedom for the latent process innovations. Defaults to Inf, which gives Gaussian innovations: a t with infinite degrees of freedom is a normal. Set df = NA to estimate them, or supply a number above 2 to fix them.

Finite degrees of freedom let the latent process absorb an occasional large shock while sigma_trend stays at the scale of ordinary variation. That suits boom-and-bust population series and outbreak dynamics. The innovations follow a multivariate t. Because it shares one innovation scale across the series at each time point, large innovations tend to occur together. Each series keeps its own direction and magnitude. A shock in one series says nothing about the sign of the others. One series can also stay unmoved by an event that moves its neighbours. cor sets the correlation between series exactly as it does for Gaussian innovations. The degrees of freedom set how heavy the tails of the innovations are.

When df = NA the degrees of freedom are estimated as nu_trend, with a default gamma(4, 0.3) prior. The prior argument replaces it, for example prior(gamma(2, 0.1), class = "nu_trend"). get_prior lists nu_trend with the other trend classes.

Three caveats apply. The bound of 2 is required. Below it the innovations have no finite variance. An autoregressive trend then has no stationary covariance to start from. Above it, the first states of an autoregressive trend take the stationary mean and covariance. Their distribution matches the stationary law exactly under Gaussian innovations alone. A finite mix of t variates has heavier tails than the infinite sum that defines that law. The degrees of freedom are informed only through the tail of the latent process. They are weakly identified in short series: below roughly 200 time points, the posterior stays close to its prior. VAR() samples its states directly and PW() has no innovations. Neither takes df.

p

The autoregressive lags. The accepted form depends on the trend type:

  • For AR() models: a positive integer or a positive integer vector. A scalar p = k is the textbook AR(k) and expands to the consecutive lags 1:k. The fit then estimates ar1_trend through ark_trend. A vector p = c(...) selects a sparse lag set. p = c(1, 12) declares only ar1_trend and ar12_trend, a seasonal AR with no intermediate lags. p = c(2, 4) declares only ar2_trend and ar4_trend.

  • For VAR() models: a positive integer. p = k is the VAR(k), with one coefficient matrix for each of the lags 1:k. A sparse lag vector is not supported. The stationary initialisation of Heaps (2023) is defined on the companion form of consecutive lags. A sparse lag set has no companion form with the same identified stationary covariance. Use AR(p = c(...)) for sparse-lag autoregression on a single series.

coef_sharing

How the coefficients of AR() vary across the latent series. "none" (the default) estimates each series' coefficients independently. "shared" estimates one coefficient per lag for every series. "hierarchical" pools each series' coefficient toward a mean for its lag, as ar{lag}_trend[j] ~ normal(mu_ar{lag}_trend, sigma_ar{lag}_trend). The section on AR coefficient sharing lists the parameters each setting samples.

Value

An object of class mvgam_trend, which contains a list of arguments to be interpreted by the parsing functions in mvgam.

Details

A trend_formula takes one trend constructor. The arguments of that constructor express richer dynamics:

  • For seasonal patterns: AR(p = c(1, 12)). A sum such as RW() + AR(p = 12) is refused

  • For several time scales: AR(p = c(1, 7, 30)) for daily, weekly and monthly lags

  • For cross-series dynamics: VAR(p = 2)

Stationarity of AR(p): a consecutive lag set with p >= 2 is sampled as partial autocorrelations, ar1_pacf_trend through ark_pacf_trend, each declared on (-1, 1). The Levinson-Durbin recursion derives ar1_trend through ark_trend from them. Every summary, forecast and hypothesis test uses those coefficients. Any vector of partial autocorrelations in (-1, 1) gives a stationary process. Bounding the coefficients directly admits explosive draws. With ar1_trend and ar2_trend both at 0.9 the declared bounds hold, yet that process grows without limit. Priors for these models name the ar{k}_pacf_trend classes.

AR(p = 1) samples ar1_trend directly. At one lag the declared interval is already the stationary region. A sparse lag set such as AR(p = c(1, 12)) also samples ar{k}_trend directly. It fixes its intermediate coefficients at zero, a constraint the recursion cannot express. It carries no stationarity guarantee. Both take priors on the ar{k}_trend classes.

CAR() steps a continuous-time AR(1) over the gaps the data records. A gap dt is measured in units of the median gap between two consecutive observations of one series. ar1_trend and sigma_trend then describe a typical step. The model is the same whatever unit the time column records. Across a gap dt the decay is ar1_trend^dt and the innovation standard deviation is sigma_trend * sqrt((1 - ar1_trend^(2 dt)) / (1 - ar1_trend^2)). The decay and the innovation scale together. The marginal variance is then sigma_trend^2 / (1 - ar1_trend^2) at every occasion of an irregular grid. The first state comes from that marginal.

CAR(cor = TRUE) correlates the innovations of several series. Sigma_trend is their covariance over a gap of one. Series a and b have stationary covariance Sigma_trend[a, b] / (1 - ar1_trend[a] * ar1_trend[b]). The innovations across a gap dt have that covariance times 1 - (ar1_trend[a] * ar1_trend[b])^dt. This is the exact transition of the continuous-time process. A time point added between two others leaves the model for the remaining times unchanged. L_Omega_trend is the Cholesky factor of the correlation between the series' shocks over an instant. Its prior is placed there. The correlation of Sigma_trend is closer to zero than that correlation when the series damp at different rates. On a regular grid the likelihood is that of AR(p = 1, cor = TRUE) with positive coefficients.

The series of a CAR() trend may be observed at their own times. The trend has a state for every series at each time any series was observed. A series contributes to the likelihood at the times it has a row. This is the model a frame gives when every unobserved time of a series has a row with a missing response. forecast() takes each series at its own future times. df needs the series on shared times. With one mixing scale per time, a multivariate t would let the times of one series change the trend of another.

Note

VAR fits and init = 0: the stationary map of Heaps (2023) takes matrix square roots by eigendecomposition. The gradient of an eigendecomposition divides by differences between eigenvalues. init = 0 in the call to mvgam() sets every raw coefficient to zero and every innovation scale to one. Each matrix the map decomposes is then the identity, with repeated eigenvalues, and the first gradient is not finite. Leave init at its default random draws for VAR() fits. AR(), RW(), CAR() and ZMVN() are unaffected.

AR coefficient sharing

Each coef_sharing setting samples its own Stan parameters:

coef_sharingStan parameters with priors
"none"ar{lag}{stem}_trend per series
"shared"shared_ar{lag}{stem}_trend (one per lag)
"hierarchical"mu_ar{lag}{stem}_trend, sigma_ar{lag}{stem}_trend

{stem} is _pacf for a contiguous lag set of two or more lags, where the sampled quantity is a partial autocorrelation, and empty for p = 1 and for a sparse lag set such as p = c(1, 3). AR(p = 2) samples ar1_pacf_trend and AR(p = 1) samples ar1_trend. Every setting defines the same ar{lag}_trend[j] in transformed parameters. Forecasting, IRF, FEVD and summaries use that quantity whatever the setting. A prior on any sampled parameter is set with brms::set_prior(class = "<name>"). get_prior(mvgam_formula(...)) lists the parameters the chosen coef_sharing samples.

Parameter Naming Convention

Every trend parameter carries a _trend suffix, which keeps it distinct from an observation model parameter of the same name. The innovation scale is sigma_trend, the moving-average coefficient theta1_trend, the autoregressive coefficients ar1_trend to ark_trend and the VAR coefficient matrices Phi_trend. Priors take these class names, as in prior(inv_gamma(5, 1), class = sigma_trend). Parameter extraction takes the same names.

Identification

A factor model with sampled loadings fits equally well under any reordering or sign change of its factors. Some models also fit equally well under any rotation. mvgam reports one version, chosen by the dynamics of the factors:

  • AR() factors take their own coefficients, as do RW() and AR() factors with ma = TRUE. A rotation would mix those coefficients. After sampling, the factors of every draw are reordered and signed to agree with one reference. The loadings Z, the factor paths lv_trend and the coefficients ar1_trend or theta1_trend move together. Factors are numbered by the variance they explain, largest first.

  • RW(), VAR() and ZMVN() factors without a moving-average term are unchanged by rotation. So are AR() factors with coef_sharing = "shared" and no moving-average term. Following Heaps & Jermyn (2024), generated quantities rotate each draw to lower-triangular loadings Z_tilde with a non-negative diagonal. The factor paths rotate to lv_trend_tilde. A VAR factor model rotates its coefficients to Phi_trend_tilde.

Post-fit methods use the identified loadings and factor paths. shared_variation() and residual_cor() are the same under every version.

A trend_map keeps its fixed entries on Z exactly. A by = lv_axis() smooth ties each factor to its own covariate effect. Neither takes a rotation. For a model with every loading sampled, the loadings_prior argument of mvgam() replaces the default iid Student-t prior on Z with a structured matrix-normal prior. That prior is built from per-series features, pairwise distance matrices or both. See mvgam for its arguments.

Setting loadings_prior = "mgp" (or loadings_prior = list(column_shrinkage = "mgp")) switches the column scaling to the multiplicative gamma process prior of Bhattacharya & Dunson (2011), which shrinks later columns of Z toward zero with increasing strength. n_lv is then a truncation ceiling on the factor count. active_factors reports the posterior distribution of the number of active factors.

References

Heaps, S. E. and Jermyn, I. H. (2024). Structured prior distributions for the covariance matrix in latent factor models. Statistics and Computing, 34:143. doi:10.1007/s11222-024-10454-0

Heaps, S. E. (2023). Enforcing stationarity through the prior in vector autoregressions. Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics, 32:74-83. (VAR stationarity prior used for VAR() trends.)

Clark, N. J., Ernest, S. K. M., Senyondo, H., Simonis, J., White, E. P., Yenni, G. M. and Karunarathna, K. A. N. K. (2025). Beyond single-species models: multispecies forecasts for ecological predictability. PeerJ, 13:e18929.

See also

get_prior() lists the parameters a trend adds and their default priors. residual_cor(), irf(), fevd() and stability() interpret fitted latent dynamics. forecast() propagates them forward. The overview vignette compares the trend types. The VAR article interprets a fitted VAR() with irf(), fevd() and stability(). The hierarchical VAR article fits gr and subgr. The dynamic factor vignette fits n_lv and trend_map.

Other trend models: LLT(), PW(), ZMVN(), list_trend_types(), lv_axis()

Examples

# \dontrun{
# A constructor records a trend before any data are seen. Printing
# one shows the settings the model will use
AR(p = c(1, 12))
#> mvgam trend specification:
#>   Type: AR({1, 12})
#>   Time variable: time
#>   Series variable: series
VAR(p = 2, ma = TRUE)
#> mvgam trend specification:
#>   Type: VARMA(2, 1)
#>   Time variable: time
#>   Series variable: series
#>   Correlated innovations
RW(gr = region, subgr = species)
#> mvgam trend specification:
#>   Type: RW
#>   Time variable: time
#>   Series variable: series
#>   Correlated innovations
#>   Hierarchical grouping: region
#>   Subgroups: species

# Three Poisson series, each surveyed at its own irregular times.
# Every series keeps about 60 percent of the occasions
set.seed(11)
simdat <- sim_mvgam(type = 6L, family = poisson(), n_series = 3L,
                    n_timepoints = 80L)
keep_some <- function(d) d[runif(nrow(d)) < 0.6, ]
own_times <- keep_some(simdat$data_train)

# The parameters a trend adds, with their default priors, before
# any fitting
get_prior(
  mvgam_formula(y ~ s(season, bs = "cc", k = 6),
                trend_formula = ~ CAR(cor = TRUE)),
  data   = own_times,
  family = poisson()
)
#>                   prior         class                        coef group resp
#>  student_t(3, 1.6, 2.5)     Intercept                                       
#>    student_t(3, 0, 2.5)           sds                                       
#>    student_t(3, 0, 2.5)           sds s(season, bs = "cc", k = 6)           
#>          exponential(2)   sigma_trend                                       
#>          normal(0, 0.5)     ar1_trend                                       
#>    lkj_corr_cholesky(2) L_Omega_trend                                       
#>  dpar nlpar    lb    ub tag       source
#>                                  default
#>                 0                default
#>                 0           (vectorized)
#>                 0                default
#>             0.001 0.999          default
#>                                  default

# A continuous-time AR(1) steps each series over its own gaps
mod <- mvgam(
  y ~ s(season, bs = "cc", k = 6),
  trend_formula = ~ CAR(cor = TRUE),
  data          = own_times,
  family        = poisson(),
  chains        = 2,
  silent        = 2
)
#> Warning: 6 of 2000 (0.0%) transitions ended with a divergence.
#> See https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings for details.
summary(mod)
#>  Family: poisson 
#>   Links: mu = log 
#> Formula: y ~ s(season, bs = "cc", k = 6) 
#>    Data: own_times (Number of observations: 109) 
#>  Series: 3 
#>  Trends: CAR 
#>   Draws: 2 chains, each with iter = 2000; warmup = 1000; thin = 1; 
#>          total post-warmup draws = 2000
#> 
#> == Observation Model ==
#> Smoothing Spline Hyperparameters:
#>                Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
#> sds(sseason_1)     1.52      0.66     0.69     3.26 1.01      750     1153
#> 
#> Regression Coefficients:
#>           Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
#> Intercept     1.58      0.09     1.39     1.75 1.00     1554     1406
#> 
#> == Trend Model ==
#> Trend Specific Parameters:
#>                       Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS
#> sigma_trend[series_1]     0.32      0.10     0.15     0.53 1.00      822
#> sigma_trend[series_2]     0.48      0.13     0.24     0.78 1.00      913
#> sigma_trend[series_3]     0.60      0.12     0.39     0.87 1.00     1135
#> ar1_trend[series_1]       0.59      0.23     0.07     0.92 1.01      540
#> ar1_trend[series_2]       0.42      0.22     0.03     0.84 1.00      615
#> ar1_trend[series_3]       0.18      0.14     0.01     0.52 1.00     1417
#>                       Tail_ESS
#> sigma_trend[series_1]      914
#> sigma_trend[series_2]      995
#> sigma_trend[series_3]     1571
#> ar1_trend[series_1]        854
#> ar1_trend[series_2]        943
#> ar1_trend[series_3]       1283
#> 
#> Draws were sampled using sampling(NUTS). For each parameter, Bulk_ESS
#> and Tail_ESS are effective sample size measures, and Rhat is the potential
#> scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, Rhat = 1).
#> 
#> Next steps:
#>   - `pp_check(fit)`: posterior predictive checks
#>   - `residual_cor(fit)`: implied cross-series correlations
#>   - `forecast(fit, newdata = ...)`: out-of-sample forecasts
#>   - `lfo_cv(fit)`: leave-future-out model comparison
#>   - `conditional_effects(fit)`: covariate effects
#> Use `how_to_cite(fit)` for a methods paragraph and `methods_md(fit)` for its equations.

# Correlations among the series' latent states
residual_cor(mod)
#> Residual correlations from an mvgam fit
#>   Source     : correlated innovations
#>   Covariance : stationary
#>   Series     : 3
#>   Mean |r_ij| (i != j): 0.21 [0.06, 0.40]
#>   Pairs with prob_nonzero > 0.95: 0 / 3

# Residual checks. Each series has gaps of differing length. A
# semivariogram by time lag replaces the ACF
plot(mod, type = "residuals", series = 2)


# Each series is forecast at its own future times
plot(forecast(mod, newdata = keep_some(simdat$data_test)),
     series = 2)


# Next: hindcast() returns the fitted latent trends. The articles
# under 'See Also' fit VAR, hierarchical and factor trends
# }
